subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Water and Food Security Reading
subtitle: Reading passages about water stress, food access, case studies, and sustainable responses.
description: This pack helps students revise why safe water and nutritious food are unevenly available across the world. It connects physical geography, human geography, real-world case studies, map skills, climate data, sustainability, and common misconceptions about water and food security.

data.sourceTitle: Why Water and Food Security Matter
data.targetTitle: Why Water and Food Security Matter
data.sourcePassage: Water and food security are not just about whether water or food exists somewhere in the world. They are about whether people can reliably get safe water and enough nutritious food where they live, at a price they can afford, and in a way that protects health and the environment over time. A household may live near a river but still lack safe water if the river is polluted or if there are no pipes, pumps, or treatment systems. A country may grow a large amount of food, but some families may still go hungry if prices are too high or markets are too far away. Geographers study both physical factors, such as climate and rivers, and human factors, such as poverty, infrastructure, conflict, and policy.

data.sourcePassage: World water stress is uneven. North Africa and the Middle East often have very high water stress because many places have dry climates, limited rainfall, and high demand. South Asia can also have high stress because large populations and irrigation create heavy demand, even though monsoon rains can be intense in some seasons. The western United States and the interior of Australia include dry or semi-dry regions where cities, farms, and ecosystems may compete for limited water. The Amazon Basin usually has low water stress because it has high rainfall and a large river system. However, water stress is not only about rainfall. Infrastructure, pollution, population, farming, and management all affect whether water is safe and available.

data.sourcePassage: In a semi-arid farming region, rainfall may be lowest during the hottest months. This pattern creates a challenge because crops often need water when evaporation is also high. If summer temperatures reach very high levels and rainfall is very low, soil can dry quickly and irrigation may be needed. A single dry week is weather, but a pattern of hot dry summers over many years is climate. Farmers use climate information to choose crops, plan planting times, and decide whether irrigation or drought-resistant seeds are needed. If winter rainfall is lower than normal, reservoirs and groundwater may not refill enough before the next growing season. This can increase the risk of water stress and food insecurity.

data.sourceTitle: Case Study: The Colorado River Basin
data.targetTitle: Case Study: The Colorado River Basin
data.sourcePassage: The Colorado River is a major river in the western United States and northern Mexico. It supplies water for cities, farms, Indigenous communities, hydropower, and ecosystems. The river flows through a dry region, and large cities such as Las Vegas, Phoenix, and Los Angeles depend partly on its water. Farmers also use river water for irrigation. Dams and reservoirs store water, but they can change downstream ecosystems. In some years, drought and high demand have lowered reservoir levels. The challenge is not only that the region is dry. It is also that many people, farms, cities, and ecosystems depend on the same limited river system. Sustainable responses include improving irrigation efficiency, reusing treated wastewater, reducing city water waste, restoring wetlands, and creating fair agreements among users.

data.sourcePassage: The Sahel is a semi-arid region south of the Sahara Desert that stretches across several countries in Africa. Rainfall is seasonal and can vary a lot from year to year. Drought can reduce crop yields, stress grazing land, and make recovery harder for communities with fewer resources. Conflict in some areas can disrupt farming, roads, markets, and aid. It is important not to describe the Sahel as one simple place where nothing grows. The region includes many communities, landscapes, cultures, and farming systems. People have adapted in many ways, including moving livestock, choosing crops suited to local conditions, harvesting water, planting trees on farms, building stone lines to slow runoff, and using pits that collect rainwater near crops.

data.sourceTitle: Cities, Food Access, and Water Management
data.targetTitle: Cities, Food Access, and Water Management
data.sourcePassage: Food insecurity can happen in cities as well as rural areas. Some city neighborhoods have few grocery stores, limited public transportation, low household income, high prices at small stores, safety concerns, or limited kitchen facilities. These areas are sometimes called food deserts, though some communities prefer the phrase low food access areas. Solutions may include farmers markets that accept food assistance benefits, community gardens, grocery delivery, better public transportation, school meal programs, and support for local food businesses. Cities can also face water security challenges. Singapore is a small, densely populated island country with limited natural freshwater. It improves water security by collecting rainwater in reservoirs, importing some water, recycling treated wastewater, desalinating seawater, and encouraging water conservation. These systems can be effective but require energy, money, maintenance, and strong management.
